extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, scientists, and investigators developing methods of empirical inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing natural history and an inductive method of scientific investigation: how to collect, publish, and interpret empirical particulars and how to proceed from experiments to axioms across the sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include common objects in natural history
rubrics_metrics.description: No judgment can be formed of that which is rare or remarkable without a previous regular examination and discovery of the causes of that which is common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect and admit the most common objects into your history: investigators must examine causes of frequent, familiar phenomena (gravity, heat, light, hardness, etc.) rather than assume them as self-evident. Failure to investigate the common has been highly injurious to philosophy because familiar objects do not arrest attention and so their causes remain unexamined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admit mean, sordid, and 'filthy' particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjects which appear mean or filthy are no less worthy of admission into natural history than the most magnificent and costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not refuse seemingly unpleasing or lowly facts: valuable knowledge can emanate from mean instances (example: fine odors from putrid matter such as musk and civet). The worthiness of a phenomenon for inquiry is its existence, not its elegance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize experiments that 'afford light' over immediate profit
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek experiments that afford light rather than profit; the aim is illumination of simple natures and access to general mysteries, not immediate material utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and value experiments for their power to clarify basic principles (the 'light') even if they seem useless in themselves; such clarity enables derivation of axioms and broad effects. Analogies: light on the first day—light is not material but enables all subsequent work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate simple natures and elemental constituents thoroughly
rubrics_metrics.description: The knowledge of simple natures, when sufficiently investigated and defined, resembles light and affords access to the sources of valuable axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze and define basic elements (the 'seeds' of substances, elemental properties) because they are the foundation from which powerful effects and general laws grow. Even scattered observations must be collected and organized to be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid speculative subtleties before establishing axioms
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtile disputes and discursive efforts are late and preposterous when introduced after the discovery of axioms; their chief opportunity is when experiment is to be weighed and axioms derived from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not indulge in abstract scholastic subtleties or word-play prior to building an empirical base; such subtleties waste effort if not grounded in experimentally derived axioms and may catch at nature without seizing her.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on authority; prioritize evidence of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject every kind of fiction and imposture and prefer the evidence of facts rather than deriving authority from ancients or genealogies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Base method and claims on observed evidence rather than deference to ancient authorities; whether a discovery was known before is immaterial compared to its factual evidence and explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay generalization until intermediate steps are completed
rubrics_metrics.description: Prohibit decisions and the laying down of certain principles until arriving regularly at generalities by the intermediate steps; aim for 'fitting certainty' not premature firmness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Restrain from premature generalizations: work through proper inductive stages, applying interpretation after preparing and arranging a history and tables of invention. Better to know what is necessary than to imagine full possession of truth prematurely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form histories and tables of invention across domains (including mind and morals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The inductive method comprehends not only natural philosophy but other sciences (logic, ethics, politics); form histories and tables of invention for passions and mental operations as well as material phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile empirical instances and systematic tables for emotions (anger, fear, shame), mental operations (memory, composition, judgment), and physical subjects (heat, vegetation). Use the doctrine of interpretation to adapt precepts for application to each subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish and preserve empirical particulars rather than only finished systems
rubrics_metrics.description: Ancients often worked from instances and commonplaces but did not publish the notes, minutes, and commonplaces. The scaffolding (empirical record) ought not to be removed when the building is finished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make empirical notes, minutes, and collections of particulars available: do not hide the underlying instances that give rise to generalizations. Transparency of the empirical base prevents dogmatic accommodation of exceptions and supports correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use deductive logic and demonstration as scaffolding, not as a substitute for experiment
rubrics_metrics.description: Forms of demonstration (syllogism) are necessary to support, verify, and extend induction but are detrimental when obtruded in the place of direct experiment or when used to deduce conclusions about nature from imaginary hypotheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ deductive forms to arrange and connect empirically derived propositions; avoid relying on à priori syllogisms to generate natural knowledge without experimental foundation. Both inductive and deductive processes have roles; misuse of deduction can systematize error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that the method levels personal talent; rely on rules and demonstration
rubrics_metrics.description: Our method of discovering the sciences levels men's wits and leaves little to superiority, since it achieves everything by the most certain rules and demonstrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design methods and rules that allow reproducible discovery independent of exceptional individual talent; attribute success more to method and circumstance than to individual acumen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value inventions and mechanical discoveries as supreme contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of great inventions is among the most distinguished human actions; inventions (e.g., printing, gunpowder, compass) can change the world more than civil or political achievements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize the pursuit of inventions that extend human power over nature: such discoveries yield wide, enduring benefits and advance human dominion by enabling arts and sciences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equate truth with utility in the pursuit of natural philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth and utility are perfectly identical: effects are of more value as pledges of truth than from the benefit they confer on men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pursue knowledge of nature as both an end in itself and as a means to useful effects: the correct model of the world in the understanding should reflect nature as it is, not as reason has distorted it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bind investigators to set aside received opinions and restrain premature generalization
rubrics_metrics.description: If men can lay aside received opinions and restrain themselves from generalization until the proper season, they may fall into the way of interpretation without the aid of any art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate intellectual discipline: suspend deference to accepted notions and avoid early generalization so that interpretation can arise naturally from a well-prepared empirical history.
